text: The Mars Desert Research Station (MDRS) is the largest and longest-running Mars surface research facility and one of two simulated Mars analog habitats operated by the Mars Society. Built in the early 2000s near Hanksville, Utah, in the western United States, the station is located on the San Rafael Swell of Southern Utah, 11.63 kilometers (7.23 miles) by road northwest of Hanksville. It is the second such analog station established by the Mars Society, following the Flashline Mars Arctic Research Station (FMARS) on Devon Island in Canada's high Arctic. The MDRS campus includes a two-story habitat with a greenhouse, a solar and robotic observatory, an engineering pod, and a science building. The Mars Society launched the Mars Analog Research Station Project to develop knowledge for human exploration of Mars, focusing on field tactics under environmental constraints, habitat design and tool testing, and crew selection protocols. Although warmer than Mars, the desert was chosen for its Mars-like terrain and appearance. During missions, crew members wear analogue space suit simulators—complete with helmet, jumpsuit, boots, gaiters, gloves, air and water packs, and a radio—when conducting extra-vehicular activities (EVAs), using hand-held radios with push-to-talk switches to communicate. EVA destinations are selected from a database and reached either on foot or by all-terrain vehicle. The station is owned and operated by the Mars Society, which selects crews and manages administrative tasks; the society is an international non-profit that collaborates with governments on projects like M.A.R.S., the Mars Analogue Pressurized Rover Competition, and the ARCHIMEDES Mars balloon mission. MDRS hosts a NASA-funded training program for teachers to simulate lunar and Martian living conditions through field research and on-site stays. Crews set individual scientific goals, with most biological research focusing on extremophiles such as bacteria and algae from the surrounding desert. Studies have identified viable methanogens in soil and vapor samples from Utah, Idaho, California, Canada, and Chile, including five soil and three vapor samples near MDRS. Crews also study endoliths—bacteria living inside rocks that photosynthesize using light penetrating the rock—commonly researched by geologists and biologists. Other experiments include heart rate and blood pressure changes during EVAs, cognitive-mood correlations, and dexterity comparisons between space suits and regular clothing. Crews typically consist of six volunteers for two-week rotations during the northern hemisphere winter, ending in northern spring due to heat. Volunteers cover their own transportation costs and are not paid. Crews include scientists, astronomers, physicists, biologists, geologists, engineers, and occasionally journalists, each assigned roles such as commander, executive officer, health and safety officer, crew biologist, crew geologist, or chief engineer. The commander oversees crew operations, maintains communication with mission support, sets daily agendas, and holds morning and evening meetings. The executive officer serves as second-in-command and takes over if the commander is unavailable. The crew geologist and biologist collaborate on mission science goals, including field planning and lab work, working with a remote science team throughout. The chief engineer maintains habitat systems such as power, water, ATV, and GreenHab operations. As of February 2017, 175 crews had served at MDRS over sixteen years. Both FMARS and MDRS began with a two-level habitat module 8 meters (26 feet) in diameter, featuring a lower level with bathrooms, labs, two airlocks, EVA prep areas, and storage, and an upper level with six sleeping quarters, a common area, computing space, and a galley. Over time, MDRS expanded significantly due to continuous use and maintenance, while FMARS remained more isolated. The MDRS expansion includes a greenhouse (GreenHab), solar observatory (Musk Observatory), science building (Science Dome), engineering pod (RAM), and robotic observatory. The Musk Observatory, named after Elon Musk who donated $100,000, houses a 28-centimeter (11-inch) Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope donated by Celestron, operated remotely and accessible via internet to amateur and professional astronomers, with support from Le Sueur Manufacturing, Software Bisque, Vince Lanzetta, Adirondack Video Astronomy, High Point Scientific, Technical Innovations, and the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Association. The modules are connected by tunnels; the lower deck hosts science and engineering activities, including a shower, toilet, biology and geology labs, two simulated airlocks, EVA prep, and storage, while the upper deck supports social activities, dining, and communications with seven crew quarters. The loft contains a freshwater tank and equipment storage, and a hatch allows access to antennas and weather instruments. Power comes from 12 rechargeable 24-volt batteries (providing up to 12 hours of power) and two 5-kilowatt generators, with power distributed via an inverter and 19 circuit breakers. Water is supplied from a 450-US-gallon (1,700-liter) tank 100 feet away, manually transported or pumped to a 60-US-gallon (230-liter) internal tank, then gravity-fed to the habitat via a pressure pump, with greywater from sinks and showers used for toilet flushing. Water is rationed and monitored to reduce waste. The habitat has an internet connection and webcams for public viewing. The original GreenHab, a closed-loop water recycling center retrofitted in 2009, was destroyed by fire in December 2014 and replaced in September 2015 after an Indiegogo campaign raised $12,540. The rebuilt GreenHab was initially planned as a geodesic dome but was completed as a 12-foot by 24-foot transparent, climate- and light-controlled structure due to wind and winter issues. It grows herbs, greens, radishes, tomatoes, and other vegetables. The engineering pod, a retrofitted Chinook helicopter fuel compartment, was moved to the campus in October 2017 and became fully operational in November 2018. North of the GreenHab is an underground septic tank and outflow field, marked as a "No Drive – Foot Traffic Only Zone" due to unknown burial location, and east of the GreenHab is an omnidirectional Jovian radio telescope. MDRS hosts the annual University Rover Challenge, first held on June 2, 2007. The flag of Mars and the United States flag appear on several buildings. The station's coordinates are 38°24′23.25″N 110°47′30.85″W.
